title: About
lead: AI-Debate is a thesis project: AI activities for homework, designed to make students think and to give teachers practical help with assessment. It is free, open source and cheap to run, even for schools with no money to spend.

origin.title: Where it comes from
origin.p1: My name is Andres Moles and AI-Debate is my thesis project. It started with one question: if students already use AI to do their homework, can we build an assignment where the AI doesn't give the answer but makes them think?
origin.p2: The six activities on this site are my attempt at an answer. Students have to convince a historical figure, interview two people who disagree, guess who is hiding behind the answers, step into someone else's shoes or moderate a debate. The characters are based on Wikipedia, so the topic can come from history, literature, science or geography.

homework.title: Why homework
homework.p1: In class there is a teacher. At home students are on their own, and more and more often they have a chatbot that can write the essay for them. Recent research points the same way: a general-purpose chatbot improves the work handed in but not what is learned, and once the help is taken away results can get worse (Bastani et al., 2025; OECD, 2026). Tools built with a teaching purpose do better.
homework.p2: AI-Debate tries to be one of them. The character doesn't do the exercise: it asks questions, pushes back, asks for evidence. Students learn by doing, inside a concrete situation, not by reading a ready-made answer (Chi & Wylie, 2014; Lave & Wenger, 1991). Every activity ends with a written reflection where students judge how it went.

assessment.title: Help for whoever grades
assessment.p1: Reading and grading thirty conversations takes hours. So at the end of each activity the AI suggests a grade with its reasons, and the student writes a self-assessment. The teacher sees the full conversation, the reflection and the suggestion, and can accept it, change it or ignore it. The grade stays the teacher's decision.
assessment.p2: The idea comes from research on formative assessment. Feedback helps when it comes early and says what to improve (Black & Wiliam, 1998; Hattie & Timperley, 2007), and judging your own work is part of learning (Zimmerman, 2002).

cost.title: Built for schools without a budget
cost.p1: Many schools can't pay a subscription for every student. AI-Debate has no subscriptions: it connects directly to the models' APIs and the school pays only for what it uses. With the free models available today, it may pay nothing at all.
cost.p2: The administrator sets a monthly spending cap. When it is reached, paid models stop and free ones keep working. Every request is logged with its tokens and cost, so you always know how much you are spending and for which class.

local.title: And one day, fully local
local.p1: The server can already use Ollama and LM Studio, models that run on a school computer without sending anything outside. Today, though, a local model good enough to hold a debate in the students' language needs hardware almost no school has. I don't know how long it will take, but small models are improving fast. When an ordinary PC is enough, AI-Debate should work that way too: no costs and no data leaving the school.

limits.title: What I don't know yet
limits.p1: I don't yet have data on how much students actually learn with these activities. The classroom trials so far are for finding bugs and checking that the activities hold up, not for proving that they work. The grade suggested by the AI can be wrong too, which is why the teacher has the last word.

code.title: The code
code.p1: The code is public on GitHub under the AGPL-3.0 license. Anyone can read it, install it on their school's server and change it, as long as they share their changes under the same license.
code.p2: The server is a single Go program with an SQLite database and installs with Docker. The repository also contains the paper “From Theory to Practice”, which describes the teaching principles behind the project.

cta.title: Try it with your class
cta.p1: Pick an activity, set it as homework and then tell me how it went: what worked, what didn't, what the students said. Teachers' reports are the most useful part of this thesis.
